attributes.title: Level 10

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you explore the image assets in My Assets?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓What images do you notice in My Assets?

❓ What might each asset be used for in this project?

❓What might the starter code for be used for in this project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to notice that the circle asset is titled emptyPaint and is transparent. Prompt the ninja to consider how this asset might be used in the project.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by exploring the assets in My Assets and the existing code in the editor. 


Click the Assets menu along the top of the screen, and notice the images stored in My Assets. Click on each asset and consider how they will be used in this project.


Return to the JavaScript editor and test out the project so far. Notice that there is a Canvas sprite, a moving Player sprite, and 6 Palette sprites. Consider what each sprite might be used for in this project.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use the Player sprite’s name and a dot operator to set the y parameter to the Player sprite’s top?
steps.instructions:
Draw on the canvas when the A button is pressed!


Click Advanced, then open Images and drag [set (picture) color at x (x) y (y) to (c)] inside the conditional in the onUpdate loop. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: picture.setPixel(0, 0, 0).


The setPixel function takes 3 parameters: x, y, and color. The x and y parameters set the pixel’s position. The color parameter sets the pixel color. 


Delete picture, then type the Canvas sprite’s name and a dot operator, and select image from the code completion tool. 


Inside the parentheses, set the x parameter to the Player sprite’s x-position. Set the y parameter to the Player sprite’s top property. Set the color parameter to any number 2-15.


Click ▶ to test out the setPixel code. Tinker with the color parameter, then the vx and vy parameters in the controller.moveSprite function to change the color and smoothness of the line.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you select 6 different colors, then type their number values in the paintColors array?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What color numbers might you store in the paintColors array?

❓ What might the paintColors array be used for in this project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to select a variety of colors from the default MakeCode Arcade palette of colors to store in the paintColors array. The ninja will explore adding colors beyond those available in the default palette at a later time.

💡 The values in the paintColors array will be used to create a palette of colors for the user to draw with.
steps.instructions:
Add additional colors to draw on the canvas with.


Find the paintColors array under // project initialization and notice that each element is set to 0. Replace each element so that there are 6 different color values, represented by numbers between 2-15, that will be used as the color palette in the project.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you change the Palette sprite’s blank pixels to the for loop’s index of the paintColors array in the replace function?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What does the replace function do? Why might it be useful?

❓ What color will be replaced in each Palette sprite? What color will each Palette sprite be set to?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The replace function replaces a specific color in an image with a new color.

💡 Remind the ninja that each emptyPaint image asset is transparent in its center. As a result, the from parameter should be set to 0, since that is the color that will be changed. As Palette sprites are created and the for loop’s index increases, a new color will be used from the paintColors array to fill the Palette sprite.
steps.instructions:
Fill each Palette sprite with a specific color from the paintColors array!


Open Images and drag [change color in (picture) from (from) to (to)] inside the for loop. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: picture.replace(0, 0).


The replace function takes 2 parameters: from and to. The from parameter is the color number of the pixels to change. The to parameter is the color number that the pixels will change to.


Replace picture with the Palette sprite’s name and a dot operator, then select im﻿age from the code completion tool. Keep the from parameter set to 0. Set the to parameter to an element from the paintColors array, using the for loop’s index.


Click ▶ to see each Palette sprite filled with a different color on screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you declare a currentColor variable, then use it to set the color parameter in the setPixel function?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why is the currentColor variable set to 1 at the beginning of the project?

❓ What pixel color is set when the A button is pressed? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The currentColor variable is set to 1 at the beginning of the project to match the color of the Canvas sprite. This will cause the Player sprite to draw an invisible line when the A button is pressed.
steps.instructions:
Prepare to change the paint color when the user overlaps each Palette sprite!


Under // project initialization, declare a currentColor variable set to 1 so the paint brush will not appear to draw until it has overlapped a Palette sprite.


In the setPixel function inside the onUpdate loop, use the currentColor variable as the color parameter, to easily update what color is drawn on screen.


Click ▶ to notice what happens when the Player sprite “draws” on the screen now.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the x and y parameters to 8 in the getPixel function?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when the Player sprite overlaps a Palette sprite?

❓ What does the getPixel function retrieve?

❓ Why should the x and y parameters of the getPixel function be set to 8?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The getPixel function retrieves the pixel color at specific x and y coordinates of an image. In this example, the function is used to find the current color of each Palette sprite. Because each Palette sprite is 16 x 16 pixels and the color that is being replaced can be found at its center, the getPixel function can use (8,8) to reliably find the current color each time.

💡 Prompt the ninja to test out the project again, noticing how they can draw in different colors by overlapping different Palette sprites.
steps.instructions:
Change the paint color when the user overlaps each Palette sprite.


Find the Player/Palette sprite overlap event under // project events. Inside, reassign the value of the currentColor variable. Open Images and drag [(picture) color at x (x) y (y)] to the right of the assignment operator. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: picture.getPixel(0, 0).


The getPixel function takes 2 parameters: x and y. The parameters get the pixel color at the x and y-positions of the image.


Delete picture, then type otherSprite and a dot operator, and select image from the code completion tool. Since the Palette sprite’s image is 16 x 16 pixels, set the x and y parameters to 8, so the currentColor is set to the color of the pixel at the center of the Palette sprite.


Click ▶ to test out the code by overlapping each Palette sprite to draw in the new colors!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you replace the brushColor with the currentColor in the replace function?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What is the brushColor variable used for? How is it different from the currentColor variable?

❓ What happens when the Player sprite overlaps a Palette sprite?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The brushColor variable stores the color of the Player sprite image’s brush tip. This should be set to 11 at the beginning of the project, to match the tip of the paintBrush image asset.

💡 When the Player sprite overlaps a Palette sprite, the Palette sprite’s color will be stored and used to replace the tip of the Player sprite’s image. The Player sprite’s color will then be reassigned. 

💡 Remind the ninja that sprite should be used (instead of the Palette sprite name) to replace the color in the Palette sprite since the code is within an onOverlap event.
steps.instructions:
Match the color of the Player sprite with the color drawn on screen!


Under // project initialization, declare a brushColor variable set to 11, the color of the paintBrush image tip.


Open Images and drag [change color in (picture) from (from) to (to)] inside the onOverlap event. Delete picture, then type sprite and a dot operator, and select image from the code completion tool. Set the brushColor variable as the from parameter, and the currentColor variable as the to parameter.


Below this, set the brushColor variable to the value of the currentColor variable, to be used for the next paint color change.


Click ▶ to see the color of the Player sprite change to match the color drawn on the screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use the setImage function to reset the Canvas sprite’s image inside the if conditional in the B button event?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What will happen when the B button is pressed?

❓ What function should be used to reset the Canvas sprite?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the B button is pressed, the screen will be “erased” by replacing the current image with the original canvasBackground image asset. Remind the ninja to use the setImage function to do this, since the background image is a sprite.
steps.instructions:
Allow the user to erase their drawing by pressing the B button!


 Under // project events create an event when the B button is pressed .


Inside the event, add an if conditional. Then, open Game and drag [ask (title)] inside the parentheses. Update the title parameter so that the user is asked if they’d like to clear the screen.


If the user responds yes, reset the Canvas sprite’s image using the canvasBackground image asset.


Click ▶ to test the code by pressing B to clear the screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you click Apply after changing the palette colors, then click ▶ to refresh the colors used in the project on screen?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ What new colors might you change the Palette sprites to?

❓ Why might you want to only change the colors used in the Palette sprites?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that there are 4 different ways to select a new color. In the Color Palette editor, the ninja can enter the 6-digit hex color code to select a specific color. This is helpful if they already know the hex color codes for a specific palette they would like to use. The ninja can also click on the color box where there are 3 additional options for selecting a specific color: the sliders, the eyedropper tool, or RGB values. If using the sliders, point out that the upper slide adjusts the color hue while the lower slider adjusts the color. If using the eyedropper tool, the ninja can hover it over any pixel on screen, even on a different tab or window, to select that pixel color. If using the RGB values, they will need to use a number 0-255 for each of the 3 values to create a different color.
steps.instructions:
Change the project’s color palette!


Return to the Assets menu, then click the Colors button under the Asset Preview window. The Color Palette editor can be used to change the 15 default palette colors by either clicking on the color box to select a new color, or by entering a 6-digit hex color code.


Use either option to change the color for each of the 6 paint colors used in the project. When prompted, give the new color palette a name, then click Apply to update the colors in the project.


Click ▶ to test the new paint colors in the project, and return to the Color Palette editor to continue exploring different color combinations!

subgroups.title: Painter’s Palette
subgroups.introduction: Create a project that allows the user to paint on the screen in different colors!

validationItems.text: Declare 2 variables to control game conditions and values in the project. Update the values in the paintColors array to store a list of 6 possible colors.
Use the setPixel function to draw on the screen when the A button is pressed.
Fill the row of Palette sprites with different colors from the paintColors array on screen.
When the Player sprite overlaps a Palette sprite, use currentColor and brushColor variables to paint with different colors on the Canvas sprite!
Erase the canvas when the B button is pressed.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 10 of Brown Belt! Before you create your final Brown Belt project, there are a few neat tricks to learn that could take your game to the next level! Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 10:

badges.title: Extension Explorer
badges.description: Use the minimap, status bar, timer, and raycasting extensions to enhance a project.

badges.title: Bird’s Eye View
badges.description: Create and pin a minimap displaying a smaller representation of sprites and the tilemap in a corner of the screen.

badges.title: Gauging the Action
badges.description: Make something happen based on the value of a status bar.

badges.title: Wait for the Signal
badges.description: Use throttle to delay an action in a game.

badges.title: Right on Cue
badges.description: Run a chunk of code after a certain amount of time has passed.

badges.title: In-Depth Image
badges.description: Create a 3D version of a tilemap from a sprite’s perspective.

badges.title: Points of View
badges.description: Toggle between 3D and top-down views of a tilemap.
